content_html:
The proof of effort

Not a day goes by when I don’t see an “interesting project” somewhere on my internet. Sometimes it’s a “news” article, sometimes it’s a reddit post, sometimes it’s something that pops up on a work channel.

It used to be that you could evaluate these things at a glance, at least to a degree. If it has a long commit history, lots of code written, in-depth documentation and a few screenshots, you could tell that some effort was made, and thus presumably something useful was built. And so it may have value to you too.

And for a while now this has not been the case, now that tech-demo-machines are effective and attainable. Putting something pretty-looking online doesn’t cost you anything. But it still takes effort to check it out. And it’s amusing, if not surprising, to see that people don’t.

A while ago, an “open-source photoshop” made the news. “A programmer rebuilt photoshop, office, outlook and what have you! On Github!” I read an article about this, and it stood out to me that it describes the projects in terms of “author says”. Author says it does X and runs on Y. Author claims it has these and those features. So the “journalist” did not even bother to run the thing, they just copied claims from the readme.

Now, that’s not a new problem. A lot of “journalism” these days is just copying stuff from press releases doing exactly zero original research and applying no critical thinking. Reposting has been professionalised. On the other hand, is it really that surprising that no one would bother to actually run the thing?

What makes you choose what software project (or art form) to engage with? It takes time, after all, to critically evaluate it. There was never enough time worth spending to try out everything that is out there, even before the slopmachines. So what makes you try X over Y?

A project popped up in a work chat today. Interesting concept at a glance, but clearly vibe-coded. The readme stating things like “why customers choose Foobator” in a project built in one day over 10 commits. The code packaged as a com.example.foobator.*. Code clearly not written by a human, and quite likely not read by a human either. I see no reason to believe that the code even works, and if the screenshots are real. It’s possible that I’ve already spent more time looking at it than the author did.

But who cares how it was built if it’s good?

In my head, I coined something called “proof of effort” as a proxy for determining whether engaging with something is worth my time, and how much of it. It’s not because I’m sitting on my high horse on top of my ivory tower, and if it didn’t involve a tired human then it’s not worthy of my ideals, no.

I firmly believe that the quality of a software project is a function of time that a human spent pushing back on it. Whether it was an engineer looking at the code and saying “this will cause problems and needs to be different” or a user saying “this feature is confusing and the UI sucks”. You can’t have a good thing without something going through a few (thousand) critical evaluation loops. Someone needs to try it out, see why it sucks, and make it better. Over, and over again.

A lot of these things are trivial, and LLM harnesses have them built in. The code likely compiles, runs without errors, names things sensibly, formats things correctly etc. Perhaps there was a human in the loop pushing back on the LLM, causing improvements. Maybe. And maybe something good came out of it, and the one-day-old 10-commit project is actually fantastic.

But I have limited time to care. And more than ever, I have virtually unlimited amount of things to check out. So my proxy for “is it worth my time” is “can I tell that human time and effort was spent on this?”

It’s not always easy to tell. You can’t rely on people’s and projects’ reputations, since so many have fallen for the vibecoding frenzy and they don’t put in any effort anymore. You may look at projects from Codeberg with more optimism than project from Github, though in my experience Codeberg does not really enforce its anti-LLM policy, even in blatantly obvious cases. Maybe you raise an eyebrow if something boasts about being “written in Rust”, in this day and age. I sure do.

And it’s okay if I miss some gem every now and again. I always have, because this problem has always been there. But if at no point in a project’s lifetime I can see pushback and disagreement, how can it possibly be good?

When has there even been a good project where every open issue was met with “an excellent suggestion!” and duly implemented?
